title: Whose wife? (Mark 12:18–27)
hook: a trick question about seven brothers; he is God not of the dead but of the living

segments.voice: Yesterday, a coin with Caesar's face on it, and your line was you bear god's image. Whose face did you see differently? Day two hundred twelve.

Another group steps up with another trap. This time it's the Sadducees, and Mark tells us straight away what they believed: they say there is no resurrection. They come with a story built to make the whole idea look ridiculous. The Law of Moses said that if a man died without children, his brother should marry the widow, so the family line would go on. So, they say: there were seven brothers. The first marries and dies, no children. The second marries her, and dies. The third. All seven. Last of all, the woman dies too. Here's the punchline, in the King James Bible: "In the resurrection therefore, when they shall rise, whose wife shall she be of them?" A story built to end in a shrug.
screen: `THE SADDUCEES: NO RESURRECTION.` → `SEVEN BROTHERS, ONE WIFE.` → `WHOSE WIFE SHALL SHE BE?`

segments.voice: Jesus doesn't laugh along. He says: "Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?" Two mistakes. First, you're imagining the life to come as this life stretched out, with the same arrangements. When the dead rise, he says, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven. God's power isn't limited to making more of the same. And notice the woman: in their story she's only a puzzle, passed down a line of brothers. He refuses to play. Second, the scriptures. Have you not read, he asks, in the book of Moses? At the burning bush, God tells Moses: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. By then Abraham was long dead, and still God names himself as his God. And then the line: "He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living." If God is still their God, they are still his. Jews in Jesus's day debated this. The book of Acts says the Sadducees denied the resurrection and the Pharisees confessed it. On this question, Jesus's answer sides with the Pharisees. Today's word, resurrection, is anastasis in Greek: literally standing up again. The Apostles' Creed puts it plainly: the resurrection of the body. How it will be, the text doesn't say. That it will be, Jesus is sure: God is the God of the living.
screen: `YOU KNOW NOT THE SCRIPTURES.` · `NOT MORE OF THE SAME.` · `STILL THEIR GOD.` · `ANASTASIS: STANDING UP AGAIN.` · then, large: `HE IS NOT THE GOD OF THE DEAD, BUT THE GOD OF THE LIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone you've lost, with hope. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind. A grandparent, a friend, a parent, even a pet if that's where your heart goes. Picture them as they were at their best. Don't rush past the ache if it's there. If you believe, you can hold them before the God of the living, and let hope sit next to the grief. If you're not sure what you believe, simply give thanks that they were, and still are, part of you. The bell holds the time.
Resurrection. In Greek, anastasis, standing up again. Jesus says God is the God of the living.
Your line: god of the living. Today, say the name of someone you've lost out loud, to someone who knew them, or just to yourself. Day two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Christians confess "the resurrection of the body" in the Apostles' Creed, and at Christian funerals this hope is often spoken over the grave; some churches remember the dead by name in prayer, especially on All Saints' and All Souls' Days.

original.note: Greek: resurrection, literally a standing up again. ana, up, and stasis, standing.

trapdoor: what you thought: resurrection means ghosts or clouds.
what it means: God is still the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so they live to him; the dead will rise, changed.
what a scholar hears: anastasis, standing up. a real debate between Pharisees and Sadducees (Acts 23:8), and Jesus argues from the burning bush in Exodus 3:6.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Cut "you can almost hear them smirking" (unfair to the Sadducees) and the unsourced claim that they leaned on the five books of Moses (now Mark 12:26's "book of Moses"). "Not I was. I am." removed: Mark's Greek has no verb there, so the tense argument overreads the text (screen head now STILL THEIR GOD); this also avoids repeating day 223's I am. "Dead for centuries" cut. Pharisee/Sadducee claim now cites Acts 23:8; the unsourced line on Jewish daily prayer cut. "Christians of every church confess it in the old creeds" narrowed to the Apostles' Creed (the Nicene Creed says "resurrection of the dead").
'The Sadducees leaned on the five books of Moses' is a common but debated claim (based partly on Josephus and patristic sources). Confirm phrasing.

Jewish neighbor line: the Amidah's second blessing praises God who gives life to (revives) the dead; stated as 'many Jews still praise God, in daily prayer'. Confirm, and that the mention is brief and non-comparative.
Pharisees taught resurrection (Acts 23:8; Josephus); confirm 'Jesus stood with the Pharisees' on this.
